Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Aerospace & Defense Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up can be found by pressing *1 on your telephone keypad. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Jordan Lee, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Jordan Lee:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Aerospace & Defense's Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Karen Ortiz, Chief Financial Officer; and Laura Kim, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Actual results could differ materially due to a variety of factors. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, Jordan, and good morning, everyone. Apex Aerospace & Defense delivered a solid performance in Q3, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across defense systems, commercial aviation, space, and aftermarket services. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering long-term value to our shareholders.

Let me start by walking through our overall company performance highlights and key takeaways for the quarter, which really underscore the resilience and growth trajectory of our portfolio. Despite ongoing macroeconomic headwinds such as supply chain disruptions in titanium forgings and inflationary pressures on labor and commodities, we executed strongly and exceeded our guidance on both top and bottom lines. Headline numbers: we reported Q3 revenue of $2.48 billion, up 14% year-over-year and 3% above the high end of our guidance range. This is our ninth straight quarter of double-digit organic growth, powered by a balanced mix of commercial ramp-ups and defense program accelerations. Adjusted EPS landed at $1.92, up a robust 22% from last year, thanks to disciplined cost management and favorable segment margins. Year-to-date through nine months, revenue is at $7.6 billion, tracking right toward our updated full-year outlook of $10.1 to $10.3 billion, with adjusted EPS of $7.45 to $7.65.

Our funded backlog reached a record $48.2 billion, up 18% year-over-year, with a quarterly book-to-bill of 1.3 to 1, giving us about 4.8 years of revenue coverage for exceptional stability amid program delays and geopolitical shifts. Free cash flow was a standout at $450 million for the quarter, up 25% year-over-year, driven by advance payments on hypersonic cruise missile contracts and working capital efficiencies in commercial aftermarket services.

Diving into segments, our Defense Systems division, representing 52% of revenue, led the way with 19% year-over-year growth to $1.29 billion. We captured a $1.2 billion low-rate initial production contract for Next Generation Air Dominance sensor suites, establishing us as a key Tier 1 supplier alongside primes like Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman. Margins expanded 210 basis points to 16.8%, reflecting higher fixed-price volumes and learning curves from F-35 Block 4 upgrades—we've delivered more than 1,200 electronic warfare modules this year. Geopolitical pressures in the Middle East and Eastern Europe sped up demand, including $350 million in Ukraine-related replenishment for JASSM-ER munitions.

Commercial Aerospace, at 38% of revenue, grew 10% to $943 million as narrowbody production recovers post-pandemic. Nacelle systems for Boeing 737 MAX and Airbus A320neo saw 15% volume increases with OEMs ramping to 38 ships per month for the MAX. Aftermarket MRO jumped 28% year-over-year from extended engine hours and our composite repair tech, cutting turnaround by 20% at San Antonio. Margins held at 14.2%, even after absorbing $25 million in one-time costs from Spirit AeroSystems issues.

Space & Advanced Technologies contributed 10% of revenue at $227 million, up 8%, highlighted by the orbital insertion of our third Responsive Space Vehicle under the Space Force's Tactically Responsive Space program, outpacing competitors on cost per kilogram. We also won a $450 million IDIQ for hypersonic glide body prototypes, building on DARPA Falcon heritage.

Operationally, we've tackled industry challenges head-on. Supply chain inflation cooled to 4% year-over-year from dual-sourcing with U.S. and allied providers like Carpenter Technology for alloys and Howmet for titanium. Our digital thread using Siemens NX and PTC Windchill digitized 85% of engineering workflows, slashing non-recurring costs 15% and speeding NGAD prototyping by six months.

Sustainability is core: we've cut Scope 1 and 2 emissions 22% year-to-date via hydrogen-blended natural gas at Huntsville test cells, aligning with DoD net-zero by 2030 and unlocking EU green procurement for low-emission satellite buses.

Regionally, North America was 72% of revenue on the $850 billion FY25 DoD topline. Europe at 15% balanced A400M delays with a €300 million Eurofighter upgrade deal amid Baltic tensions. Asia-Pacific grew 25% on P-8A Poseidon for India and RQ-4 UAS expansions in Japan. Middle East added 4% via Saudi Vision 2030 munitions backlog.

Strategically, our $1.2 billion R&D—12% of revenue—drives GaN-based AESA radars with 40% range gains for the $25 billion global market through 2030. Partnerships like our RTX JV on directed energy and Blue Origin MOU for reusable structures diversify space revenue.

Q4 guidance is $2.65 to $2.75 billion revenue and $2.10 to $2.20 adjusted EPS. For 2025, we see 11-13% growth to $11.2-$11.5 billion with EBITA margins at 15.5-16.0%. Risks like Boeing strikes or shutdowns are offset by our backlog, 35% cash-to-debt, and M&A dry powder in cyber-electronics. In short, unmatched visibility, margin gains through cycles, and a pipeline for great power competition and air travel rebound confirm our fortress balance sheet and tech leadership—we've grown 45% since pandemic lows, beating peers, with $300 million buybacks and 1.8% dividend yield.

Building on that momentum, a standout story this quarter was our major new contract awards and program wins, which propelled our funded backlog to a record $48.7 billion, up 28% year-over-year and offering over 4.5 years of revenue visibility at current rates. Our book-to-bill expanded to 1.8x from a mix of U.S. DoD primes, international FMS, and commercial space breakthroughs. These validate our leadership in contested logistics, hypersonics, and collaborative combat aircraft, positioning us for share gains in a 5.2% CAGR global A&D market through 2030 amid great-power rivalry, per Teal Group.

In Defense Systems, we booked $12.4 billion—double last year's Q3 pace. We're prime for the U.S. Air Force's Increment 2 Collaborative Combat Aircraft program: a $4.2 billion five-year IDIQ for low-cost attritable UAVs teaming with NGAD, using our AI autonomy from Skyborg. Prototyping ramped at Mojave with 95% mission success in Yuma demos against hypersonic threats, beating Boeing and General Atomics via MOSA that cuts integration 30% per GAO.

We also got a $3.1 billion fixed-price U.S. Army deal for Block 2 AH-64E Apache upgrades—1,200 aircraft with next-gen Longbow radar, multi-spectral targeting, and JADC2 integration. Q1 2025 deliveries from Mesa, Arizona, 85% domestic content for Berry Amendment, tying into Indo-Pacific tensions and AUKUS for allies like Australia, Japan.

Missiles: $2.8 billion from Navy NAVAIR for LRASM Block 2 and hypersonic seekers—our tandem warhead ups lethality 40% vs. A2/AD, validated at Pacific Missile Range. Scaling hypersonic tunnels at White Sands for HIMARS ER follow-ons post-ARRW pivot.

Internationally, now 22% of backlog up from 15%, a $1.9 billion FMS with Poland for 48 F-15EX Eagle II with Rampage missiles and AESA upgrades. Poland's $40 billion modernization post-Ukraine favors us over Saab Gripen; 2026 St. Louis deliveries with Polish MRO offsets creating 1,200 jobs.

Middle East: $1.2 billion UAE for THAAD reloads and DEW turret prototypes—150kW laser hits 99% kill at 5km vs. drone swarms at Gulf Test Range, countering Houthis. Diversifies from U.S. sequestration as Gulf funds $150 billion through 2028 per SIPRI.

Space & Launch: $1.7 billion NASA/DoD for 36 SDA Tranche 2 Tracking Layer satellites with Hall-effect thrusters for refueling in proliferated LEO—20% cost edge via additive manufacturing and COTS photonics, topping Northrop, Millennium. Plus $800 million OneWeb Ka-band, surging space backlog 45% to $6.2 billion in the $100 billion New Space economy.

Our fortress portfolio: 60% recurring sustainment, R&D up 18% to $1.2 billion for quantum-resistant JADC2 encryption. Supply chain 92% U.S., dual-sourced GaN semis despite China risks. New program margins 14-16% EAC, FY25 guidance raised to $28-30 billion revenue, 12.5% operating margins assuming CR resolution. Executing in 6% global defense growth to $2.4 trillion per IISS, de-risking to $40 billion backlog by year-end.

Next, on our book-to-bill ratio overall and by segment—a critical leading indicator in our industry where programs span 5 to 15 years from award to full-rate production. Above 1.0x signals strong demand and backlog growth, fueling multi-year revenue and free cash flow.

For the quarter, we hit an overall 1.18x, up sequentially from 1.12x in Q1 and from 1.05x last year Q2—$4.2 billion new orders vs. $3.55 billion revenue, adding $650 million to funded backlog at record $78 billion, up 12% year-over-year. Mix of fixed-price development, cost-plus incentives, IDIQ tasks, boosted by Eastern Europe/Indo-Pacific tensions accelerating DoD/allied spend under FY24 NDAA, plus commercial recovery despite supply issues.

By segment: Defense Systems (55% revenue) at 1.28x with $2.1 billion awards—$850 million sole-source Army PrSM Lot 7 like Lockheed extended-range, $450 million F-35 Block 4 sensors with RTX, €320 million UK MoD hypersonic prototypes under AUKUS Pillar 2. Up from 1.15x YoY, backlog $42 billion +18%; digital engineering twins cut design 25% via MBSE for NGAD bids, H2 milestones.

Commercial Aviation (25% revenue) at 0.98x, $850 million bookings vs. $865 million billed—soft widebody from Boeing 737 MAX certs/Airbus A350 ramps, offset by CFM LEAP aftermarket. $300 million Delta/LATAM 787 wingbox; Asia-Pacific +35% on China C919/IndiGo A320neo, Europe 0.85x on Ryanair delays. Up from 0.92x sequentially, H2 >1.0x as OEMs stabilize; $18 billion backlog, 40% SAF-certified take.

Space & Missiles (15% revenue) strong 1.35x, $650 million vs. $480 million—NASA $280 million Artemis IV Orion module, $220 million NSSL Phase 3 Lane 2 Vulcan Centaur upper stage vs. ULA/SpaceX, Blue Origin $150 million New Glenn adapters. UAE $120 million hypersonic testbed +50% YoY. $12.5 billion backlog +22%, reusable tech cuts launch 30% per kg.

Aftermarket & Services (5% revenue) 1.05x, $600 million vs. $570 million—15% MRO utilization growth on C-130J/F-16, AI PHM platform $100 million USAF IDIQ for readiness.

Full-year book-to-bill 1.15-1.20x on $15-18 billion expected awards like JADC2, Joby eVTOL. Risks: OTA slips, Ukraine titanium; 42% domestic content mitigates inflation. Sets up 8-10% 2025 organic growth, 12-14% ROIC.

We're particularly excited about recent advancements in our Collaborative Combat Aircraft program and its potential to drive future growth through attritable UAVs teaming with next-gen fighters. Strong demand persists for defense systems, and commercial aerospace is steadily recovering.

Karen Ortiz:
Thank you, Michael. Now, let's turn to the financials. In Q3, we reported revenue of $2.48 billion, representing a 14% increase year-over-year. Our adjusted earnings per share were $1.92. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $4.2 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year remains unchanged at $10.1 to $10.3 billion in revenue and adjusted EPS of $7.45 to $7.65. We're actively managing costs while investing in growth initiatives like hypersonics and digital engineering. We're also committed to returning capital through our dividend and $300 million in share repurchases this year.

Specific highlights: gross margin of 22.1%, up 180 basis points; operating income of $425 million, up 20%; free cash flow of $450 million.

Before questions, let me detail the key assumptions underlying our full-year 2025 guidance, which we reiterated at 7-9% organic revenue growth to $82-84 billion, adjusted EPS $28.50-$29.50, and free cash flow $6.5-7 billion. This draws on our $168 billion backlog, up 4% year-over-year, targeting mid-single-digit margins expansion via execution and efficiencies. Subject to 10-K risks like geopolitics and supply chains.

Macro: U.S. GDP 2.0-2.5% per IMF, inflation 2-2.5%, 10-year Treasury 3.75-4.25%. FY25 NDAA at $895 billion DoD topline +3.5%, Army $185 billion, Navy $257 billion shipbuilding. Geopolitics: $25-30 billion Ukraine aid at 60% munitions; Middle East $1.2 billion Iron Dome/David's Sling; NATO 2% GDP by 23/32 allies for F-35/Patriot; Asia 5-7% despite China rare earths, offset by AUKUS. Shutdown/CR sensitivity: 1-2 point revenue headwind.

Missiles & Defense (45% revenue): 10-12% growth to $37 billion. JASSM-ER/LRASM 650 units/year on $4.1 billion multi-year; 95% on-time via Oklahoma fab +25% capacity. Hypersonics $2.5 billion ARRW Phase 3/GPI TRL-6; 15% CAGR on $12 billion DoD budget. International 20%: Poland Wisla Phase 2, UAE THAAD $800 million. Titanium $25/kg -10% YoY, electronics 20 weeks; digital twins cut SRM scrap 18%, +150 bps margins. Sensitivity: Ukraine cuts -$500 million, Taiwan offsets.

Aeronautics (30%): flat-2% to $25 billion. F-35 Lot 18-19 156 aircraft $11 billion; TR3 Q1 2025, 110-120 Lot 19, $6 billion sustainment +12% ALSS via ODIN. Classified B-21 LRIP $4 billion, NGAD $1.2 billion. Middle East Israel F-35A $3 billion, Qatar upside. Mexico composites 40% F-35 empennage -15% costs RTM. Sequestration 50 bps EPS hit.

Space Systems (15%): 8-10% to $12.5 billion. GPS IIIF 2/month $1.8 billion, Nova SDA Tranche 2 75% win PWSA. Next-Gen OPIR PDR Q4 $3.2 billion, HBTSS 2026 IOC. 30% international Golden Dome/AUKUS. Phased-array 92% yield +200 bps EBITDA. NASA SLS minor; DoD cuts -$300 million.

Commercial Aviation Aftermarket (10%): mid-teens to $8 billion. LEAP-1B 25k cycles $2.5 billion, 85% utilization. Boeing inventory 4,500; San Antonio CFM56 +25% throughput. APAC 40% IndiGo/Air China; Europe Ryanair lag. GTF issues cap $200 million.

Overarching: $1.2 billion Enterprise Excellence savings (Lean Six Sigma/GenAI) 60% to bottom; 18-20% backlog conversion, 40% fixed-price. IDIQs: $22 billion JADC2, $10 billion NGAD with RTX/Northrop. Embeds 2% revenue buffer for inflation, $5-7 billion upside supplements/exports. Targets 10%+ ROIC, $10 billion FCF to 2027.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Instructions for asking a question: press *1. Our first question comes from Chris Bennett with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Chris Bennett:
Good morning, thanks. Can you provide more color on the ramp-up timelines for the major new contract awards, particularly the CCA and Apache programs?

Michael Reynolds:
Certainly, Chris. On CCA, we've already ramped prototyping at Mojave and hit 95% success in Yuma demos, with initial deliveries under the $4.2 billion IDIQ starting late next year as we integrate AI autonomy fully. For Apache Block 2, Mesa line is tooled for Q1 2025 first flights, scaling to 1,200 units with JADC2 waveforms—geopolitics like Indo-Pacific will pull forward allied variants. These de-risk execution and bolster our 4.5-year visibility.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Sarah Kline with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Sarah Kline:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about the book-to-bill outlook by segment, especially commercial aviation where it was sub-1x—any risks to H2 recovery?

Karen Ortiz:
Sarah, great question. Overall FY book-to-bill stays 1.15-1.20x on $15-18 billion bids. Commercial at 0.98x this quarter reflects widebody softness but sequential gains position >1.0x H2 as Boeing/Airbus stabilize—Asia-Pacific strength on C919/IndiGo offsets Europe. Backlog $18 billion with SAF components gives confidence, mitigated by 40% domestic content vs. titanium risks.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Torres with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Mike Torres:
Thanks. Regarding the key assumptions underlying the guidance, particularly supply chain and hypersonics—what's the biggest sensitivity?

Michael Reynolds:
Mike, supply chain assumes titanium at $25/kg and 20-week electronics, with dual-sourcing and digital twins buffering inflation—sensitivities like Ukraine aid cuts hit munitions $500 million but Taiwan/ supplements offset. Hypersonics baked in $2.5 billion bookings on ARRW/GPI success and $12 billion DoD budget, with 95% delivery rates from fab expansions. Overall, 2% revenue buffer ensures resilience.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation in hypersonics, autonomy, and space.

Jordan Lee:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our Q3 2024 earnings call. A replay and transcript will be available on our investor relations website.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
